d: Clean water + pinch of salt + handful of sugar or honey. Dysentery and cholera stop killing most victims.
w: Unknown. Diarrhea is treated with bleeding and herbs.

d: Isolate the sick for 40 days. Needs authority, not technology.
w: Lepers are isolated, but true quarantine starts in 1377 (Ragusa).

d: Sailors and soldiers stop dying of scurvy on long trips.
w: Scurvy isn't understood; long sea voyages are rare.

d: Stop lead pipes, lead-sweetened wine and mercury 'medicines'.
w: Unknown. Lead pots and mercury cures are common.

d: Lye + fat, boiled. Already known in places; make it cheap and universal.
w: Exists. Syria and Spain make good hard soap; most people rarely use it.

d: Boil or bake clothes. Lice spread typhus, the great killer of armies.
w: Lice are normal life; nobody links them to typhus.

d: Distill wine strong enough to clean wounds and tools.
w: Salerno doctors distill 'burning water', but treat it as medicine, not cleaner.

d: Works on day one; months to make it a habit. Semmelweis cut childbirth deaths ~18% to ~2%.
w: Disease blamed on bad air and imbalanced humors. Ale is safer than water by accident.

d: Clean hands, clean cloths, trained midwives. Mothers and babies survive.
w: Midwives learn by apprenticeship; no idea of germs.

d: Tourniquets, splints, sorting the wounded. Soldiers survive and return.
w: Barber-surgeons, cautery with hot iron, little organization.

d: Clear bottles in full sun for 6 hours. UV kills germs.
w: Unknown.

d: Simple rule, big digging job. Ends most waterborne disease in a town.
w: Romans knew sanitation; most medieval towns have lost it.

d: Find cowpox on a dairy farm, scratch it into the skin. Smallpox immunity.
w: Unknown. Smallpox is everywhere.

d: Cats, traps, sealed granaries. The key to surviving the Black Death (1347).
w: Unknown. Black Death arrives 1347.

d: Drain swamps, nets over beds. Malaria drops.
w: Malaria blamed on 'bad air' (mal aria) from swamps. Close, but no.

d: Lets people SEE germs. Turns germ theory from a claim into proof.
w: Reading stones (magnifying lenses) exist. No microscope.

d: Alcohol + sulfuric acid, gently heated. Painless surgery 600 years early.
w: 'Soporific sponges' soaked in opium and mandrake; risky and weak.

d: From seaweed ash. Wound antiseptic and goiter cure.
w: Burnt seaweed and sponge are used for goiter, without knowing why.

d: Telling is instant; getting doctors to believe it takes years of proof.
w: Four humors (Galen) and bad air rule medicine everywhere.

d: Mix drops of blood on a plate to test matches. Safe transfusions.
w: Unknown. Bloodletting is a common treatment.

d: Mold is easy to grow; concentrating useful doses is the hard part.
w: Moldy bread on wounds is folk medicine in some places.

d: Blacksmiths can make them now. Faster harvests, deeper plowing.
w: Europe has the heavy plow, horse collar and some scythes.

d: Plants seeds in rows at the right depth. Less seed wasted.
w: China has had seed drills for 1,000+ years. Europe sows by hand.

d: Seal food in jars, boil. Armies and sailors eat year-round.
w: Food kept by salting, smoking, drying and pickling.

d: Clover fixes nitrogen for free. Yields roughly double, but it takes a few seasons to show.
w: Europe uses three-field rotation (wheat, beans, fallow). No clover cycle.

d: Bones + sulfuric acid. Paired with clover, yields jump again.
w: Manure and marl only.

d: Planned breeding of crops, horses, cattle and sheep using Mendel's rules.
w: Breeders select horses and dogs by eye; no theory.

d: Potato and maize. Needs a voyage to the Americas first.
w: No one in Europe, Asia or Africa knows the Americas exist.

d: Unbreakable with only paper. Frequency analysis breaks enemy codes.
w: Simple letter-swap ciphers. Arab scholars already know frequency analysis.

d: How Venice and Florence ran trade empires. Catches theft and waste.
w: Italian merchants are just inventing it (first records ~1300).

d: Teach the clerks first. Arithmetic, trade and taxes get far easier.
w: Standard in India and the Islamic world. Fibonacci brought them to Italy in 1202.

d: Front, side and top views to scale. Anyone can build to a plan.
w: Master masons sketch cathedral plans, but no standard drawings.

d: One meter, one kilogram for everyone. Required before mass production.
w: Every town has its own foot, pound and bushel.

d: Clerks compute them once; afterwards multiplication becomes addition.
w: Unknown (Napier, 1614).

d: Count people and harvests. Insurance, taxes, and proving medicines work.
w: Rare head counts for taxes (England's Domesday Book, 1086).

d: The engineer's calculator for 350 years.
w: Unknown. Abacus and counting boards.

d: Taught to a first class of students. Pays off in engineering and orbits later.
w: Unknown. Indian mathematicians have early pieces of it.

d: Test, measure, write it down, repeat. A generation of trained thinkers.
w: Alhazen (Cairo) used experiments; Grosseteste at Oxford is starting to.

d: Inventors get rewarded, so they share instead of hiding secrets.
w: Guilds guard secrets; Venice's patent law comes in 1474.

d: Pool money and risk. Funds voyages, mines and factories.
w: Italian merchants share voyage risks informally; partnerships, no stock companies.

d: Rag paper is just arriving in Europe. Scale it up.
w: Common in the Islamic world and Spain; Italy's first mills open ~1260s.

d: Movable metal type + oil ink + screw press. Spreads every other idea 100x faster.
w: China prints with wood blocks; Korea casts metal type in 1234. Europe copies by hand.

d: Relay riders on fixed routes. Letters, orders, news.
w: The Mongols' horse relay (Yam) is the best in the world. Europe uses messengers.

d: Fast to start; a full generation before it pays off.
w: Church and cathedral schools for few. Universities at Bologna, Paris, Oxford.

d: Any part fits any machine. Unskilled workers build complex things.
w: Unknown. Every item is handmade.

d: Towers + telescopes + a code book. Messages cross a country in hours.
w: Beacon fires for warnings only.

d: Silver salts on paper in a camera box. Maps, records, propaganda.
w: Camera obscura is known (Alhazen). No way to fix the image.

d: Battery + wire + electromagnet + Morse code. Instant long-distance messages.
w: Unknown.

d: Spark-gap transmitter + simple receiver. Talk to ships and armies far away.
w: Unknown.

d: Silk or paper + fire. Aerial scouting over a medieval army.
w: China has paper sky lanterns, a tiny version of the idea.

d: 75% saltpeter, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur. The wait is growing the saltpeter.
w: China uses it in war (bombs, fire lances). Europe hears of it ~1240s-1260s.

d: Wet, press and break into grains. Burns far faster and more evenly.
w: Unknown; arrives ~1400s.

d: Paper or iron tubes of powder. Terror weapon and signal flares.
w: China fires rocket 'fire arrows' at the Mongols in 1232.

d: Bells are already cast; cannon use the same skill.
w: Not yet anywhere; first true guns ~1280s-1320s. Bell-casting skill exists.

d: Spiral grooves in the barrel. Accurate at 5x the range.
w: Unknown. Crossbows and longbows rule.

d: Nitroglycerin soaked into diatom earth. Mining and canals 10x faster.
w: Unknown.

d: Soak wood ash, boil down. Base for soap and glass.
w: Common.

d: Known to a few monks and alchemists. Make it standard.
w: Known to alchemists and Salerno doctors; small-scale.

d: Manure, urine, straw and ash rot for about a year, then leach out crystals.
w: China and (soon) Arab chemists know saltpeter. Nobody farms it.

d: Lime + volcanic ash. Harbors, bridges, roads.
w: The Roman recipe is lost; lime mortar only.

d: Pure sand + soda/potash + lime. Venice already leads; push optical quality.
w: Venice and Syria make fine glass; cathedrals use stained glass. Clear, flat glass is rare.

d: Burn sulfur over water in a lead room. The master industrial chemical.
w: Alchemists make tiny amounts by heating vitriol.

d: Limestone + clay baked very hot. Concrete anywhere, no volcano needed.
w: Unknown.

d: Saltpeter + sulfuric acid. Explosives, dyes, photography.
w: Alchemists' 'aqua fortis', in tiny amounts.

d: Bake coal sealed. Coke for iron, gas for lamps, tar for later chemistry.
w: England digs 'sea coal'; China uses coal for iron. No coke in Europe.

d: Salt + sulfuric acid, roasted with limestone and coal. Glass and soap at scale.
w: Made by burning seaweed and desert plants.

d: Disinfect water, bleach cloth. Later by electrolysis of salt water.
w: Cloth is bleached with sun and sour milk over weeks.

d: Phosphorus from urine or bone ash. Fire anywhere, instantly.
w: Flint and steel.

d: Electric arc burns air into nitric acid. Fertilizer and explosives; needs a dam's power.
w: Unknown.

d: Electrolysis of alumina. Once worth more than gold.
w: Unknown as a metal.

d: Simple recipe, brutal engineering: ~200x air pressure. Feeds half of humanity today.
w: Unknown.

d: Exact recipe ratios for chemistry and coinage.
w: Goldsmiths and moneychangers have good balances.

d: Rub three plates in rotation; all three become truly flat. Precision from nothing.
w: Unknown.

d: Invented ~1286 anyway. Old craftsmen keep working for decades.
w: Invented in Italy ~1286, about 50 years later.

d: Glass tube + mercury or alcohol. Furnaces, chemistry, fevers.
w: Unknown.

d: Tube of mercury. Weather forecasting and proof of vacuum.
w: Unknown. Most scholars think a vacuum is impossible.

d: Two lenses in a tube. Wins battles at sea and on land.
w: Unknown (1608).

d: Accurate time for factories, science and astronomy.
w: Water clocks and candles. Al-Jazari's (1206) are marvels. Mechanical clocks ~1280s.

d: Simple piston pump. Unlocks steam science, bulbs, X-rays.
w: Unknown.

d: One plug must fit, one must not. The secret of interchangeable parts.
w: Unknown.

d: Pull metal through smaller and smaller holes. Electricity needs miles of it.
w: Done by hand through draw-plates for chain mail and jewelry.

d: Melt steel in clay pots. Hard cutting tools and springs.
w: India's wootz and Persia's 'Damascus' steel are crucible steel. Europe can't make it.

d: The mother machine: it can cut a screw better than its own.
w: Simple pole lathes for wood; screws are cut by hand.

d: Prism + slit. Identify metals in ore by their light.
w: Unknown.

d: Cuts truly round cylinders. Made the steam engine work.
w: Unknown.

d: Small pump, enormous force. Forging and high-pressure chemistry.
w: Screw presses for wine and oil.

d: Mills already exist. Belt one wheel to a whole room of machines.
w: Mills are everywhere (5,600+ in England by 1086), grinding, fulling cloth, hammering iron.

d: Horse carts on wooden rails. One horse pulls 10x the load.
w: Unknown in Europe until the 1500s.

d: Cheap cast iron in quantity. No more forests burned for charcoal.
w: Early charcoal blast furnaces in Sweden; China far ahead with cast iron.

d: Crude and forgiving. Pumps water out of mines.
w: Unknown. Hero's steam toy is forgotten.

d: Separate condenser: 3-4x more efficient. Powers factories.
w: Unknown.

d: Blow air through molten iron. Cheap steel by the ton.
w: Unknown.

d: High-pressure engines on wheels.
w: Unknown.

d: Armies and goods move across the country in days.
w: Unknown.

d: Ships ignore the wind.
w: Unknown.

d: Copper and zinc discs with salt-water cloth between. The catch: pure zinc is rare in 1200s Europe.
w: Unknown. Static sparks and lodestones are curiosities.

d: Insulated wire around iron. The base of motors and telegraphs.
w: Magnetic compass exists in China and Europe; magnetism is a mystery.

d: Coat metals in copper, silver or gold. Rust-proofing and wealth.
w: Gilding uses gold dissolved in toxic mercury.

d: Split compounds: sodium, potassium, pure copper.
w: Seven metals known: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, mercury (zinc in India).

d: Spin coils of wire near magnets. Electricity from a waterwheel.
w: Unknown.

d: Blinding light for lighthouses and forts.
w: Oil lamps, tallow and wax candles.

d: He knows where coal, iron, copper, tin and silver lie. 'Dig here.'
w: Miners follow surface signs and luck.

d: Compass, charts, latitude by stars, trade winds and currents.
w: Compass is new; sailors hug coasts. Portolan sea charts appear ~1270s.

d: Falling pressure = storm. Farming, sailing and battles.
w: Folk sayings and astrology.

d: Stern rudder, mixed sails, better hulls. Reach any coast.
w: Europe sails cogs; the sternpost rudder is new. Chinese junks are bigger and better.

d: Potatoes, maize, silver, rubber, quinine.
w: Vikings reached Newfoundland ~1000, then forgot.

d: Instant prophet power, if he remembers the dates. Halley's comet: 1222, 1301.
w: Astronomers predict eclipses roughly. Comets are seen as omens.

d: Samalas erupts 1257; Great Famine 1315-17. Store grain, look like a prophet.
w: Famines are blamed on fate or sin; no warning.

d: Fix the Julian calendar's drift. Accurate seasons and festival dates.
w: The Julian calendar is ~7 days off the sun and drifting.

d: No perpetual-motion projects; design efficient engines on purpose.
w: Heat is thought to be an element (fire).

d: Ends alchemy. Predicts which elements exist and how they act.
w: Four elements: earth, water, air, fire. Alchemists chase gold.
